beats.text: Right now, as ChatGPT writes its answer to you, it has no idea how its own sentence is going to end.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace
beats.chapter: No plan, one word at a time

beats.text: It doesn't plan the paragraph. It doesn't even plan the next sentence. It picks one small piece of a word, then the next, then the next.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And yet about a billion people use it every week, to write emails, fix code and explain homework.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So how can something that is basically guessing, one word at a time, sound so smart? Let's open the box.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: First, ChatGPT doesn't actually read words. It reads tokens.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A token is a chunk of text. Sometimes a whole word, sometimes just a piece of one. On average, a hundred tokens make about seventy-five English words.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Every token is turned into a number, because underneath it all, the model can only do maths.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: This one detail explains a famous fail. For a long time, chatbots insisted the word "strawberry" has only two R's.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Why? Because the model never saw the letters. It saw a couple of token chunks, like "straw" and "berry", each one just a number.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Counting letters inside those chunks is surprisingly hard for it, a bit like counting the letters in a word you only ever heard spoken. Newer models that work step by step usually get it right.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So when you type a question, ChatGPT sees a long row of numbers. And its only job is to answer one question about them.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: What token is most likely to come next?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: You already know this trick. It's the autocomplete on your phone keyboard. Type "I'll be there in", and it suggests "five minutes".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: ChatGPT is that same idea, scaled up enormously. For every next token, it calculates a probability for tens of thousands of options.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Then it picks one, adds it to the text, and does the whole thing again. Word, by word, by word.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's also why you can ask the same question twice and get two different answers. ChatGPT usually doesn't take the single most likely token. It rolls the dice a little, so the writing sounds natural instead of robotic.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.merge: It rolls the dice a little

beats.text: And here's something most people don't realise. Every single time ChatGPT adds one token, it looks back over the entire conversation so far.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Your question, its own earlier words, everything. That's how it keeps track of what "it" or "that" refers to.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: BEFORE EVERY NEW TOKEN, IT LOOKS BACK AT

beats.text: The technique that makes this possible is called attention. It was introduced by Google researchers in twenty seventeen, in a paper called "Attention Is All You Need". It's the T in GPT: the transformer.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Attention lets the model decide which earlier words matter most for the next one. In "I dropped my laptop and now it won't start", attention links "it" back to "laptop", not "I".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

msgs.text: I dropped my laptop and now it won't start

beats.text: But there's a limit to how much it can look back on, called the context window. In a very long chat, the earliest details can get less attention, or fall out completely. That's why it sometimes forgets what you said at the start.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.label: CONTEXT WINDOW · ILLUSTRATION
v.title: A very long chat
v.hi: The earliest details can drop out

beats.text: But how does it know which guesses are good? It learned by reading. An enormous amount of reading.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: During training, the model is shown huge amounts of text from books, websites and code, with the next word hidden.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: It guesses. It checks the real answer. And it adjusts itself a tiny bit to guess better next time.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Those adjustable parts are called parameters. Think of them as knobs. GPT-3, back in twenty twenty, had a hundred and seventy-five billion of them.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Repeat that guessing game billions of times, and something surprising happens. To predict the next word well, the model has to pick up grammar, facts, styles, and even some reasoning patterns along the way.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A model trained only on the internet is a bit like a very well-read parrot. Ask it a question, and it might just continue your sentence, or ramble.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

msgs.text: What is the capital of India?
What is the capital of France? What is the capital of…

beats.text: So companies add a second stage. Real people write good example answers, and rank the model's answers from best to worst.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The model is then trained to produce the kind of answers people prefer. This is called reinforcement learning from human feedback.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And it matters a lot. In OpenAI's twenty twenty-two study, people preferred answers from a small model trained this way over the giant GPT-3, a model a hundred times bigger.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: OPENAI STUDY, 2022 · MODEL SIZE (PARAMETERS)
v.src: Source: OpenAI, Training language models to follow instructions (2022)

beats.text: Now here's the catch. Remember, its job is to produce a likely-sounding next word, not a true one.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Most of the time, likely and true are the same thing. But when the model doesn't really know, it can still produce something that sounds perfectly confident. That's called a hallucination.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: OpenAI researchers compared it to a student on a multiple-choice exam. If you get zero points for saying "I don't know", guessing always looks smarter.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And many of the tests used to grade AI models work exactly like that. They reward a lucky guess more than an honest "I'm not sure".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's why rare facts are where it slips most: a specific date, a small company's details, a quote from a person who isn't famous. There's no strong pattern to predict from.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So is ChatGPT just fancy autocomplete, or does it actually understand?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Honestly, researchers still disagree. It clearly isn't thinking the way you do. It has no memory of your life and no experience of the world.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But predicting text really well turns out to require surprisingly deep patterns. That's why it can explain code, translate languages and solve problems it has never seen word for word.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: A useful way to think about it: it's an incredibly well-read prediction machine. Powerful, but not a source of truth on its own.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.who: Powerful, but not a source of truth on its own

beats.text: Once you know how it works, you can use it much better. Here are four habits.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: One. Give it context. The more relevant details you put in, the better its predictions become. "Write an email" is weak. "Write a polite email to my manager asking for Friday off" is strong.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: 4 HABITS FOR BETTER ANSWERS
v.detail: "Write a polite email to my manager asking for Friday off"

beats.text: Two. Give it permission to say "I don't know". Simply adding that one line to your question can reduce confident made-up answers.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Three. Check anything that matters. Facts, numbers, dates, legal or medical advice. Ask for sources, then open them yourself.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: 4 HABITS FOR BETTER ANSWERS
v.detail: Ask for sources, then open them

beats.text: Four. For hard problems, ask it to work step by step. Writing out the steps gives the model more text to build on before it reaches the answer.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.title: 4 HABITS FOR BETTER ANSWERS
v.detail: More steps = more text to build on

beats.text: So, ChatGPT doesn't know what it's going to say next. It predicts it, one token at a time, using patterns from an enormous amount of human writing.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: That's what makes it so useful, and also why you should never switch your own brain off.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

v.text: Never switch your own brain off.
